(CNN) — Iranian human rights activist and Nobel laureate Shirin Ebadi has joined the legal team representing Roxana Saberi, an Iranian-American journalist convicted of spying and imprisoned in Iran.

Ebadi, a prominent civil rights leader in Iran and the 2003 Nobel Peace Prize recipient, took on Saberi’s case at the request of Saberi’s family, her father, Reza Saberi, told CNN on Wednesday. Ebadi heads the Center for Defenders of Human Rights in Iran.

Saberi, 31, was sentenced Saturday to eight years in prison following a one-day trial that was closed to the public. President Obama, along with other U.S. and international officials, sharply condemned the verdict.

The Rev. Jesse Jackson has offered to travel to Iran to help seek Saberi’s release.

“If our voices are heard in Iran today, I would be anxious to travel with a delegation to Iran, if we are permitted, and make an appeal for her freedom,” the longtime civil rights activist said, according to his Rainbow PUSH Coalition.

Jackson, 67, spoke Tuesday at a peace conference in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

“Whenever we’ve brought people out of captivity, whether in Syria, Cuba, Iraq or Yugoslavia, or Liberia, it’s always opened a diplomatic door to reduce tensions,” he said.

Saberi’s attorneys said they will appeal her conviction. Judiciary Chief Ayatollah Hashemi Shahroudi has ordered the head of Tehran’s Justice Department to ensure that the appeals process is swift and fair.

Jackson has previously offered to help secure the release of American hostages, most recently in 2005. At that time, he said he was willing to use his role as a religious leader to help secure the release of Roy Hallums, who was kidnapped along with five others in Baghdad in November 2004. Hallums was freed in September 2005 when U.S. troops raided the farmhouse outside Baghdad where he was being held.

In 1984, Jackson secured the release of a Navy pilot held in Syria. In 1991, he helped secure the release of 500 “international guests” held in Iraq. In 1999, he persuaded Yugoslavia to release three U.S. soldiers detained during the Kosovo conflict.

Obama has called for Saberi’s release, saying he is “gravely concerned with her safety and well-being.”

“We are working to make sure that she is properly treated, and to get more information about the disposition of her case,” Obama said Sunday. “She is an American citizen, and I have complete confidence that she was not engaging in any sort of espionage.”

Iranian officials initially said Saberi had been detained for buying a bottle of wine. The Foreign Ministry later said she was being held for reporting without proper credentials.

Saberi, who is from North Dakota, has lived in Iran since 2003, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists, a journalists’ advocacy group. She has worked as a freelancer for National Public Radio and other news organizations and was writing a book about Iranian culture.

Iranian authorities revoked her press credentials in 2006, but Saberi continued to file short news items without permission, the journalists’ group said.

Saberi was detained in January, though no formal charges were disclosed at the time. On April 9, reports emerged that she had been charged with espionage.

“Without press credentials and under the name of being a reporter, she was carrying out espionage activities,” Hassan Haddad, a deputy public prosecutor, told the Iranian Students News Agency.

Authorities also said Saberi had confessed. Her father said he believes she was coerced into making damaging statements.

CNN’s Shirzad Bozorgmehr contributed to this report.

The accusations later escalated dramatically, with Iranian prosecutors alleging she had gathered classified information and passed it to U.S. intelligence services.

Her one-day trial, held behind closed doors in Tehran’s Revolutionary Court, resulted in a conviction for espionage. The sentence was announced in April, shocking her family, press freedom groups and U.S. officials, who have repeatedly denied that Saberi was involved in spying.

Ebadi’s involvement could bring new attention to the legal irregularities surrounding the case. She has long criticized Iran’s judiciary for political prosecutions and lack of due process, and her participation signals that Saberi’s defense will challenge not only the espionage charge but also the way the case was handled.

U.S. officials called for her release and said the espionage accusation was baseless.

But human rights organizations, including Reporters Without Borders and the Committee to Protect Journalists, have condemned the conviction, calling it politically motivated and part of a broader crackdown on journalists and dual nationals.

Her dual nationality complicated the case: Iran does not recognize dual citizenship and treats Iranian-Americans as Iranian nationals under its legal system.

The appeal will be closely watched as a test of Iran’s judiciary and of the political climate surrounding foreign journalists and dual nationals. For Saberi’s supporters, Ebadi’s involvement offers renewed hope that the conviction can be overturned or the sentence reduced.
